newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Tax, budget doubts overshadow Russia-IMF talks.
newsitem.headline: Tax, budget doubts overshadow Russia-IMF talks.

text.p: Doubts on tax collection and next year's budget are overshadowing talks between Russia and the International Monetary Fund as the Fund debates whether to grant a new tranche of a three-year $10 billion loan.
Sources close to the discussions said on Monday that the IMF was worried about low Russian tax collection.

"The problem is not that they say that we are off track, but that they will say that the review is not finished, and until they finish the review, they cannot recommend giving us the credit," said one Russian official, who asked not to be named.
"They had no problems with any of the Russian figures except low revenues. Revenue was low in September and it was even lower in October."
Another expert said delays in approving the 1997 budget could also make life difficult for the IMF.
"It is already October and people just cannot seem to agree on a macro-economic framework and there are differences on what both revenue and expenditure should be," he said.

The State Duma lower house of parliament rejected the government's draft 1997 budget last week. It is not yet clear when the government will re-submit the spending plans, which had envisaged a deficit of 3.3 percent of gross domestic product.
An IMF delegation arrived in Russia last week for the latest monthly monitoring mission. They are due to leave at the end of this week.

Finance ministry figures show the September budget deficit was on track at 3.8 percent of gross domestic product under the methods the IMF uses to calculate the gap. The IMF target for the whole of 1996 is 5.3 percent.
Economists agreed that the deficit was on track, but said this had been achieved by cutting expenditure sharply, rather than by bringing in forecast revenues.
"They are crunching back on expenditure and a pretty savage cutting of expenditure is taking place," said one analyst.
Low tax collection is just one element of a vicious circle of non-payments affecting the whole Russian economy.
The government says the fact that companies do not pay their tax bills means it cannot afford to pay its own bills, and millions of workers go unpaid for months.
One tax debtor, oil company Tatneft, used official tax exemptions to settle 365 billion roubles of tax debts.
Tatneft was issued the exemptions because it provided oil and fuel to the agricultural sector on credit on behalf of the government, for which it has not yet been paid.
Tatneft was one of six big companies threatened with bankruptcy last Tuesday as the government tried to clamp down on alleged large-scale tax evasion.
The government said at the time that Tatneft owed it 407 billion roubles in taxes, but Tatneft chief executive Rinat Galeyev said its tax debt was only 42 billion roubles.
Tax exemptions can be used to settle tax bills, but they produce no real revenues for the government.
